scenarios.title: The Film You Hate
scenarios.text: The coaches pull up your college film in a dark meeting room, and it looks completely different from how you remembered it: slower, stiffer, younger. Someone pauses on your worst kick.

choices.label: Write down every flaw
choices.result: Every flaw the coaches point out goes on a list. It's a long list, two pages, and you laminate it and keep it in your kicking bag all season.

choices.label: Fix one thing a week
choices.result: One flaw a week, fixed and charted. By midseason, the old film looks like someone else's, and {coach} uses it to teach the rookies.

choices.label: Call your college coach
choices.result: Your college coach watches the same film that night and calls back laughing: he always knew about the plant foot. You talk for an hour.

scenarios.title: Your Parents in the Stands
scenarios.text: {parent} drives eleven hours to see you kick in person for the first time as a pro. He arrives a day early, in his old team jacket, with a cooler of sandwiches.

choices.label: Spend every minute together
choices.result: Every free minute, together: the hotel breakfast, the walk around the stadium, the sandwiches. He doesn't stop smiling all weekend.

choices.label: Give him the full tour
choices.result: The full tour: the locker room, the field, the coaches. He shakes {coach}'s hand twice and tells the equipment manager about your peewee days.

choices.label: Stick to game-week habits
choices.result: Your routine stays exactly the same, and you see him after. He understands completely, and you wish, driving home, that you'd done more.

scenarios.title: The Sibling Who Wants to Visit
scenarios.text: {sibling} wants to spend spring break at your apartment: a week of sleeping on your couch, eating your food and seeing what the league is like up close.

choices.label: Take him everywhere
choices.result: Everywhere, all week: practice, the team cafeteria, the stadium at night. {sibling} thinks you're the coolest person alive, and says so to everyone.

choices.label: Put him to work
choices.result: Your youth clinic gets a volunteer for a week, and {sibling} turns out to be great with the kids. You see him differently after it.

choices.label: Say not this year
choices.result: Not this spring, you explain; it's too busy. {sibling} is disappointed, goes to a friend's beach house instead, and sends you a photo of the ocean.

scenarios.title: The College Teammates' Chat
scenarios.text: Your old college teammates' group chat is on fire: everyone wants inside stories from the league. Who's mean, who's rich, who's actually funny. They're asking you by name.

choices.label: Tell the funny ones
choices.result: The funny stories, yes; the private ones, never. The chat loves you, and {best_friend} starts calling you 'the insider' in every single message.

choices.label: Keep the team private
choices.result: The team stays private, you explain. It's a little awkward, and it's right, and two old teammates respect it more than they say.

choices.label: Mute the chat
choices.result: Muted for the season. You miss some good jokes, and come back in January to four thousand messages and a nickname you'll never shake.

scenarios.title: The Old Flame
scenarios.text: Someone you dated in college messages you the week your first big headline runs. It's friendly, a little nostalgic, and it's the first time you've heard from them in two years.

choices.label: Meet for coffee
choices.result: Coffee, an hour that turns into three. It's warm and a little strange, you're glad you went, and you both leave it there.

choices.label: Ask yourself why now
choices.result: Why now? You don't answer it, even to yourself, and keep things friendly from a distance. The messages fade by the end of the month.

choices.label: Leave it on read
choices.result: Left on read. It's simpler, and on bad nights you wonder about it for a minute before you fall asleep.

scenarios.title: Your First Bad Practice Week
scenarios.text: Five bad practices in a row, and the coaches have stopped saying 'next one'. On the sixth day, nobody says anything at all, which is worse.

choices.label: Strip it back with {coach}
choices.result: {coach} strips your routine back to the basics: three steps, one thought, no extras. It's humbling to start over, and by Thursday it works.

choices.label: Kick until it's back
choices.result: Every night, until the field lights come on, until it's back. Your leg is heavy, and the sixth bad practice never comes.

choices.label: Talk it through with {holder}
choices.result: {holder} has seen this before and says so over coffee: everybody hits the wall once. It helps more than the kicking.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Car
scenarios.text: A veteran tosses you his keys after practice and asks you to move his car. It costs more than your parents' house, it's parked on a slope, and it's raining.

choices.label: Move it very carefully
choices.result: Very, very carefully. He notices how carefully, and from then on he calls you by your name instead of 'kicker'.

choices.label: Ask what it cost him
choices.result: What did it cost, and would he do it again? His answer is long and honest, and it's about much more than the car.

choices.label: Hand the keys back
choices.result: Not comfortable driving it, you admit. He laughs, moves it himself in the rain and tells the story at lunch, kindly, with you as the sensible one.

scenarios.title: Learning to Cook
scenarios.text: Your first apartment, and your diet is cereal, takeout and whatever the team cafeteria sends home with you. The nutritionist has started looking at you sadly.

choices.label: Learn five meals
choices.result: Five meals, learned and cooked on rotation. Your energy in practice is better within a week, and you can make a very good omelet.

choices.label: Start a cooking night
choices.result: A Sunday cooking night with two rookies and {backup}. Everyone burns something, the fire alarm goes off twice, and nobody cares in the slightest.

choices.label: Sign up for a meal service
choices.result: A meal service, expensive and perfect. You never think about food again, never learn to cook, and the delivery driver knows your schedule better than you.

scenarios.title: The Team Nutritionist
scenarios.text: The team nutritionist reviews three days of what you've eaten, one page at a time, and doesn't hide her reaction to the gas station burritos.

choices.label: Follow her plan
choices.result: Her plan, to the letter. You feel better by week two, and she puts a gold star on your locker, which you pretend to hate.

choices.label: Ask for a kicking plan
choices.result: A plan built for kicking power, strict and specific. It's hard to follow and it works, and your leg feels heavier in a good way.

choices.label: Change breakfast
choices.result: Breakfast, and only breakfast, for now. It's a start, she says, and she means it kindly, and you notice the difference by Friday practice.

scenarios.title: The Sleep Study
scenarios.text: The club puts every rookie through a sleep study, and your results are embarrassing: five hours a night, phone in your hand until two, a bedtime that moves around like the wind.

choices.label: Fix your sleep
choices.result: Every recommendation: a dark room, no phone, the same bedtime. Your practices improve within two weeks, and you dream again.

choices.label: Just go to bed earlier
choices.result: An hour earlier, nothing fancier. It helps a lot, and your phone still comes to bed with you, which the sleep coach pretends not to know.

choices.label: Compare results at lunch
choices.result: Everyone's results are terrible, it turns out. You laugh about it for a week, and the rookies start a 'lights out by ten' bet for push-ups.

scenarios.title: The Team Psychologist
scenarios.text: The club's team psychologist stops you in the hallway and offers you a standing Tuesday appointment. No pressure, they say; most of the veterans have one.

choices.label: Take the Tuesday slot
choices.result: Tuesdays at two, every week. Some weeks you talk about kicking; most weeks you talk about everything else, and that's the point.

choices.label: Say you're fine
choices.result: Fine, you say, and you are, mostly. The psychologist leaves the door open with a small nod, and the Tuesday slot stays empty for weeks.

choices.label: Build a routine with them
choices.result: The sessions become a workshop for your pre-kick routine: breath, count, one thought. It's the best thing you do all year.

choices.label: Pick up where you left off
choices.result: What worked in college goes straight to the psychologist in the first session, so the two of you skip a month of getting to know each other.
choices.lock_text: having worked with a sports psychologist in college

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Doesn't Make It
scenarios.text: The rookie you came in with is released after his first season. By noon his locker is empty, his nameplate is in the trash, and his parking spot already has someone else's car in it.

choices.label: Help him pack
choices.result: His things, carried to the car with you. He thanks you for being the only one who came, and you both pretend not to be upset.

choices.label: Kick harder
choices.result: Harder than you've kicked all year, that afternoon, alone on the far field. The empty locker is still there in the morning when you come in.

choices.label: Ask your agent what would have saved him
choices.result: What could have saved him? Your agent's answer is a list: the weight room, the meetings, the attitude. You take every item seriously.

scenarios.title: The Practice-Field Fan
scenarios.text: A kid watches every practice from behind the fence with a cardboard sign that has your name on it, spelled almost right. He's been there every day for two weeks.

choices.label: Go sign the sign
choices.result: Over to the fence after practice, and you sign the sign, fixing the spelling. He's there every day after that, beaming.

choices.label: Get him onto the field
choices.result: One kick on the real field, arranged with the club. He talks about it for years, and so do his parents.

choices.label: Wave every day
choices.result: A wave, every day, and you keep walking. He waves back every day with the whole sign, and by October the sign is spelled right.
